context: Covariance under one ratio admits many families. Scale-space theory singles out a family by a principle about what smoothing may do to an image. On the line the principle is the classical one that smoothing creates no new local extrema. Their number does not grow with scale, and this selects among the families of the line \prog{V-selection v0.1}{\S4}. Images live in the plane, and there the principle fails. One step of smoothing can raise the number of local maxima, even across an octave step of the Gaussian ladder (Figure~\ref{fig:theory-creation}). A pyramid for images therefore needs a principle that holds in the plane and can be stated on its octave steps. Section~\ref{ch:matern} gives one, and finds the family it selects.

This paper rests on five releases of the author's earlier work, cited at the printed number and page. The line paper \progpaper{V-line v0.1} states the axioms on the line and classifies the families that satisfy them. Two companion papers were released with it. The isotropic paper \progpaper{iso v0.1} carries the axioms and the classification to $\RR^d$. The affine paper \progpaper{affine v0.1} supplies the frame families, which the supplement uses for the separability of the classical kernels.

What remains of non-creation in the plane is non-enhancement: smoothing does not raise a local maximum or lower a local minimum. Its classical form requires $\partial_tu \le 0$ at a spatial local maximum of the record, which needs a derivative in scale \prog{V-selection v0.1}{Thm.~4.2(3), p.~30}. A pyramid has no derivative in scale, only its octave steps. Read at one finite step from $s$ to $t$, the principle requires $(u_t - u_s)/(t - s) \le 0$ at each weak local maximum of the later record $u_t$. This is the implicit Euler discretization of the classical form. It needs no continuum of scales, so it can be required of an octave step. A step of a family from scale $s$ to scale $t$ is its \emph{stage} $\mu_{s,t}$, and the octave step from $t$ to $qt$ is the stage $\mu_{t,qt}$, an \emph{octave stage}.

The two forms select different families. On the line, the derivative form required at every scale selects the Gaussian ray, the families whose exponent is $a\omega^2$, \prog{V-selection v0.1}{Thm.~4.2(3) and Cor.~4.4, pp.~30, 33}. Among the symmetric rotation-invariant laws, the finite-step form holds exactly for the Helmholtz resolvents $(I - \tau\Delta)^{-1}$, $\tau \ge 0$, the identity among them. It rejects every Gaussian stage $N(0, 2aI)$, $a > 0$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:stage-lemma}(3) and Theorem~\ref{thm:selection-stratum-two}(4)). \begin{itemize} \item Definition~\ref{def:implicit-euler-principle} states the finite-step principle, on the continuum and on a lattice. \item The stage lemma, Proposition~\ref{prop:stage-lemma}, finds the laws that have it. Stratum~2 holds many families, so a designer still needs a reason to choose one. On the line the count of local extrema gives that reason \prog{V-selection v0.1}{\S4}. In the plane a bound on the value at a local maximum takes its place. Among the isotropic families covariant under $q$, the \Matern{} pyramid is, up to the gauge, the one whose every octave stage has the implicit-Euler maximum principle (Theorem~\ref{thm:selection-stratum-two}(2)). Its octave step is one Helmholtz resolvent, the law $L_{ct}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:matern-pyramid}). The difference of the levels $t$ and $qt$ is $-c^2t^2$ times the Laplacian of the coarser one (Proposition~\ref{prop:laplacian-pyramid}). So for this family the level difference of the Laplacian pyramid of Burt and Adelson \cite{burt1983laplacian}, taken on the continuum before any decimation, is a Laplacian.

\emph{The selection does not count extrema.} In the plane the number of local maxima of a record is not monotone in scale for any candidate treated here: at every rung of the \Matern{} and frame \Matern{} pyramids, and at some rung of the Gaussian ladder (Proposition~\ref{prop:creation-plane}). Theorem~\ref{thm:selection-stratum-two} selects by a bound on the value of the output at a local maximum. The counting statements that select on the line \prog{V-selection v0.1}{\S4} are not offered as properties of a pyramid in the plane.

(2) The primitive $f = C + \int_0^xf'$ is continuous and bounded by $|C| + \|f'\|_1$, so $u(qs) = (\mu_s * \mu_{s,qs}) * f = \mu_{s,qs} * u(s)$ at every point, by Fubini's theorem for a bounded measurable function. By Fubini's theorem on $[0,x] \times \mu_s$, $u(s)(x) = u(s)(0) + \int_0^x(\mu_s * f')$, so $u(s)$ is the primitive of the integrable $\mu_s * f'$. The counting clause \prog{V-selection v0.1}{Prop.~4.5(2), p.~35} (Theorem~\ref{thm:cited-A23}), applied to the family $t \mapsto \mu_{t,qt}$ of $G$ at scale $s$ and the signal $u(s)$, gives $S^-(u(qs) - \alpha) \le S^-(u(s) - \alpha)$ for every $\alpha$, and $S^-(\partial_xu(qs)) \le S^-(\mu_s * f')$. By the Lebesgue differentiation theorem $\partial_xu(s) = \mu_s * f'$ almost everywhere, and $S^-$, a count in the essential sense, does not see the null set; so the right side is $S^-(\partial_xu(s))$.
Like every counting reading of non-creation \prog{V-selection v0.1}{\S~6, p.~67}, the proposition is a statement on the line.

Lindeberg's discrete scale space is exact but not a pyramid (Proposition~\ref{prop:lindeberg-stratum-one}), since its grid is a preferred length. The grid refinement that makes it covariant, the geometric-jump pyramid of Proposition~\ref{prop:discrete-gaussian-pyramid}, lies in stratum (2) of Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-line} and not in stratum (3), and its kernels are no longer lattice laws. Lindeberg characterizes the discrete Gaussian as the unique discrete kernel with non-creation and a semigroup law [\sscite{lindeberg1990scalespace}]. Without the semigroup law, non-creation leaves a class of kernels in place of one family \prog{V-selection v0.1}{Remark~4.15}. No non-creation property is claimed here for the geometric-jump pyramid. The next proposition shows that neither of the line's two tools, lattice counting and \Polya{} frequency, applies to it.
